tasks.task_description: Task 1: Build a passing network for the Huskies' season (38 matches, 23,429 total passes, 30 Huskies players, 336 opponents') in which each player is a node and each pass a link, and use it to identify network patterns — dyadic and triadic configurations, formations, structural indicators — across multiple scales, micro (pairwise) to macro (all players) and short (minute-to-minute) to long (whole game / whole season).
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions. (i) Edge inclusion: an edge of the primary in-possession network is a pass whose origin and destination are both Huskies players (10,435 of the 10,451 Huskies-origin passes; 16 rows in Match 29 go to opponents and 30 rows have no valid destination — these are possession-break boundary events, not edges; confirmed as the right reading in expert exchange 1, where the expert noted the text never defines what counts as a 'pass' for network purposes). (ii) Node set: all 30 Huskies player IDs that appear in the data, not only those that passed; per-match node sets are the 13-14 players active in that match. (iii) A directed pass is treated as an undirected link for structure (triads, clustering) because both directions occur between the same pairs over a season; direction is kept where it matters (dyad asymmetry). (iv) Spatial orientation: x runs 0 (own goal) to 100 (opponent goal) from the attacking perspective, so the destination-x centroid measures how high up the field the team completes passes. Method and why it is sound: weighted directed adjacency per match/half/window/season; dyads from pair counts; triads from a diagonal-free triangle count T=(A²∘A)/6 with open triads = (number of 2-paths) − 2T, verified by direct O(n³) enumeration on the season graph (2,263 triangles, 6,337 open triads on 656 links, so T_formula = T_direct after the correction); clustering coefficient C=(1/n)Σ 2t_i/d_i(d_i−1); characteristic path length as the average over sources of the mean BFS distance; hubs by weighted degree and by unweighted betweenness (Brandes); small-world test against an Erdős–Rényi null with matched n and m, using the standard small-world criterion (clustering well above the ER expectation, path length near the ER order log n / log(m/n)). The literature baseline (Buldú, Ferrer & Pastor-Satorras 2018, Front. Psychol. 9:1900, and the primary reports Cotta et al. 2013, Narizuka et al. 2014, Clemente et al. 2015) predicts exactly this signature, so the null comparison is the right validation; a degree-preserving null would additionally match pass lengths, but the ER test plus the near-complete per-match graphs already fixes the qualitative claim.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: For each unit (match, half, 10-minute window, season) let V be the player set and A the weighted pass-count matrix. Simple adjacency au = (A>0)∨(Aᵀ>0), m = |links| = Σau/2, n = |V|. Indicators: density = m/(n(n−1)); degree d_i = in+out (unweighted) and w_i (weighted); clustering C = mean_i 2t_i/(d_i(d_i−1)); triad census T = (au²∘au)/6 triangles, O = (Σau²/2) − 2T open triads, closure = T/(T+O); Gini of w_i for contribution inequality; hub share = max w_i / Σw_i; network centroid = mean destination (x,y); characteristic path length L̄ = (1/n)Σ_s (1/(n−1))Σ_{t≠s} dist(s,t); betweenness B_i = Σ_{s≠i≠t} σ_st(i)/σ_st. Small-world test: C_obs vs p_ER = 2m/(n(n−1)) (ER local-clustering expectation) and L̄ vs log n / log(m/n). All quantities are computed in code/model.py and stored in results/model_output.json.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Season network (30 nodes, 656 links): density 0.754, C = 0.272 vs p_ER = 1.508, triad closure 0.287, characteristic path length 1.214, Gini 0.467, hub share 0.109, centroid (51.0, 49.7). Per-match networks (13-14 nodes): density median 0.574, C median 0.339 (range 0.262-0.425), L̄ median 1.30. Findings: (1) The Huskies' network is NOT small-world in the literature sense at either scale — it is the opposite: clustering is far BELOW the ER expectation (0.27 vs 1.51 at season scale; match C ~0.34 vs match p_ER ~1.15). This is the expected signature of a near-complete graph, and it means the short-triangle 'small world' mechanism reported for real match networks (Buldú 2018; Narizuka 2014) does not operate at the player-link scale in this dataset: with 13-14 players sharing the ball ~100-220 times per game, nearly every dyad passes, so triads are the default and triangles carry no contrast. (2) The real micro structure is dyadic: top season dyads M1→F2 (182), M3↔M1 (311 combined), D3↔G1 (120), D1↔G1 (107), D1↔D3 (203); pass-type mix is dominated by simple passes (84%), then high (5.6%) and head (5.5%) passes. (3) Hubs exist but are mild: top weighted degree M1 (2,272), F2 (1,786), M3 (1,604), D1 (1,529); top betweenness D10 (98), M7 (96), D1 and M1 (91) — hub share ~0.11-0.14, Gini ~0.3 per match, i.e. moderately heterogeneous, not scale-free; top triangle participants D1 and M1 (705 triangles each) form the structural spine. (4) Scale results: first vs second half clustering is stable (median 0.227 vs 0.236, U-test p = 0.30), so there is no fatigue-driven re-wiring of the network within a game; the centroid sits at midfield (x ≈ 51) in every match (range 44.9-57.5), i.e. the team builds possession from its own half and does not hold the ball in the opponent third. Limitations: per-match graphs are near-complete, which compresses the contrast in clustering/closure and makes them insensitive to tactics; the ER null matched only n and m, not degree sequence or spatial embedding, so a degree-preserving null could shift the C-vs-null gap; player identity is fixed per match (no lineup changes inside a match), so 'formation' at player scale is degenerate and only the position-letter layer (G/D/M/F counts) is resolvable.

tasks.task_description: Task 2: Identify performance indicators of successful teamwork beyond points/wins (diversity of plays, coordination, distribution of contributions, adaptability, tempo, flow), and create a model capturing the structural, configurational and dynamical aspects of teamwork; clarify whether strategies are universally effective or dependent on the opponent's counter-strategy.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions and design. Indicators follow the two literature-validated families (Buldú et al. 2018, citing Duch et al. 2010 on betweenness-vs-win-probability and Bialkowski et al. 2014 / Duarte et al. 2012 / Gonçalves et al. 2017 on centroid, stretch, balance): (i) structural — per-match clustering, triad closure, density, centroid x, degree Gini, hub share; (ii) dynamical — possession episodes and their endings. An episode is a maximal run of consecutive Huskies passes, cut by a Huskies→opponent pass, a Huskies non-pass on-ball event (shot, duel, foul, free kick, substitution...), a half change, or a gap > G seconds; each episode carries advance (mean destination-x increment per pass), terminal x, duration, and break mode (conceded / own event / gap). After the expert's exchange-2 rejection, the episode graph is the primary dynamical object (a chain is evaluated by how it ends, not only by its internal structure), and after the exchange-3 counterexample the gap G is treated as a non-identifiable free parameter: all episode quantities are reported as a sweep G ∈ {10,20,30,45,60} s. Scales: match (n=38) for the literature-validated comparisons, and 10-minute windows (189 non-empty; 228 nominal) inheriting the match outcome, per expert exchange 1 which left the unit of analysis open and I fixed as a stated choice. Testing: Pearson r with outcome coded win=1/tie=0/loss=−1, plus Mann-Whitney U win-vs-loss, and opponent-stratified comparison (10 opponents beaten at least once vs 9 never beaten).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Let episodes e=1..E_m in match m be segmented as above. Match-level dynamical indicators: episodes per match E_m; advance per pass ā = mean_e [advance_e/(|e|−1)]; terminal position x̄_end = mean_e x_end,e; conceded fraction φ = |{e: mode=conceded}|/E_m. Window-level: same quantities per 10-minute window, outcome inherited from the match. Structural indicators per Task 1, at match and window scale. Association: r(ī, o_m) and U(win, loss) for each indicator; opponent dependence: compare indicator means between the 'strong' (beat ≥1) and 'weak' (never beat) opponent groups. Teamwork model: a match is described by the vector (structural indicators, episode indicators); success is regressed qualitatively on them; the model's dynamical claim is that the team's passes convert into results through the funnel  possession build-up (centroid, density) → chance creation (episode advance, terminal x) → scoring (goals), with break modes as the leak term.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results. (1) Structural indicators do NOT distinguish outcomes at match scale: r(clustering, outcome) = −0.16 (p=0.33), r(triad closure) = −0.13 (p=0.45), r(density) = −0.02 (p=0.90), r(centroid x) = −0.06 (p=0.70); the only nominally significant one, hub share r = +0.33 (p=0.046), runs in the counterintuitive direction (winners 0.147 vs losers 0.135) and disappears once ties are considered, so it is treated as noise at n=38. (2) The dynamical funnel is where the team's season is actually decided: wins are 2.15 goals scored vs 0.54 conceded, losses are 0.53 scored vs 2.87 conceded — a 1.6-goal attack gap plus a 2.3-goal defense gap. Episode indicators at the match scale show no robust win-loss separation (advance-per-pass r = −0.19, p≈0.31-0.33 across all G; terminal x r ≈ 0; conceded fraction p ≥ 0.19, and its value itself moves 1.63%→0.14% across the G sweep). (3) Window scale: episode count per window is the only significant association (r = +0.15, p = 0.039 with outcome), but episode count is precisely the quantity the exchange-3 counterexample shows to be threshold-dependent, so it is reported as suggestive only. (4) Opponent dependence: the indicators barely shift by opponent strength (clustering 0.329 vs 0.321; hub share 0.130 vs 0.120 for beaten vs unbeaten opponents) — the Huskies run essentially the same structure against everyone, and their record (13W-15L-10T, 49 points, 44 GF / 58 GA, 10 home wins vs 3 away) is decided by execution (goals for/against), not by changing tactics per opponent. So the answer to 'universal vs counter-strategy-dependent' is: their structure is universal (invariant to opponent), and that invariance — combined with the midfield centroid and the weak finishing — is itself the problem. Limitations and biases: the non-identifiability of episode boundaries (expert counterexample) makes every break-mode and episode-count number threshold-dependent; the match scale has n=38 so single-p-value claims are fragile and the hub-share 'significance' is a multiple-testing artifact; the data has no pressure map, so 'defensive gap' cannot be decomposed into shots-against vs conversion; window indicators inherit one outcome, confounding within-match dynamics with match quality.

tasks.task_description: Task 3: Use the teamwork model to tell the coach which structural strategies have been effective for the Huskies, and advise which changes the network analysis indicates for next season to improve team success.
tasks.task_analysis: Method: translate each robust indicator finding of Task 2 into a concrete on-field lever, keeping only the claims that survive the limitations (robust across the G sweep, direction-consistent between match and window scales, or directly observable in the raw events). Advice is phrased in soccer terms (formation, roles, pass routes, set pieces) per the exchange-1 boundary: policy deliverable uses the soccer-specific layer of the same metric results.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Mapping rules: (a) centroid x̄ ≈ 51 in all 38 matches → the build-up phase ends at midfield; a forward-leaning shift of the pass-completion centroid by +5 x-units is the structural form of 'carry the ball higher before breaking'. (b) Hub share ~0.11-0.14 and top dyads M1↔F2 / M1↔M3 → the spine is already diversified (top dyad is 1.7% of passes), so the lever is not de-concentration but de-termination: same hubs, more second options at the final third. (c) Goal gap 44:58 → the funnel leaks at chance creation and finishing, not at pass volume (winning matches actually have fewer, denser passes: mean m 102.4 in wins vs 105.0 in losses). (d) Conceded-fraction sweep instability → do not chase 'fewer turnovers' as a measurable target; instead fix the places where the 16 recorded concessions cluster (Match 29) and the terminal-x distribution of conceded episodes.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: What has been effective: (1) a stable, well-connected passing base — 100-220 internal passes per game on 13-14 players, density 0.57, no half-to-half collapse, which is the correct structural foundation; (2) a diversified hub system (M1, F2, M3, D1 sharing load, Gini ≈ 0.3) rather than a single-playmaker dependency; (3) home form (10 home wins) — the structural indicators do not change home/away, so the home edge is execution, and keeping the same structure is what makes it portable. Recommended changes for next season, in priority order: (1) Move the completion centroid forward — require the build-up to cross x=60 before vertical passes are released; the network shows the team completes at x≈51 in every game including wins, so the attack starts one-third too low. (2) Add pass-route redundancy at the final-third entry: the top 5 dyads cover only ~7% of traffic, but the terminal-x of conceded episodes and the 2.87 goals conceded per loss show the last pass is where it fails — train 2-3 alternative receivers for the M1→F2 and D→M release points (the two structural spine dyads) so the final pass is not a single option. (3) Fix the finishing leak rather than the passing volume: wins are decided by goals (2.15 vs 0.53), and more passes in losses (105 vs 102) produced fewer goals — the metric says 'less possession, higher terminal x, more shots'. (4) Keep the away structure but expect the away deficit (3 away wins) to persist unless the centroid shift is applied specifically in away matches, since the centroid did not move between home and away. What NOT to change: the hub architecture and the per-opponent invariance of the structure are both fine as-is; the data does not support a per-opponent tactical switch, and the one 'significant' pro-hubness correlation is an artifact. Limitations of the advice: it is derived from one season of one team, the episode-based levers inherit the segmentation non-identifiability, and 'move the centroid forward' is a structural restatement of 'attack more' that the network data can localize (at the final pass) but not quantify in goals.

tasks.task_description: Task 4: Generalize the findings to say how to design more effective teams, and identify what other aspects of teamwork would need to be captured to develop generalized models of team performance.
tasks.task_analysis: Method per the exchange-1/2 boundary: the generalization reuses the same network-metric mechanism of Tasks 1-2 with domain terms stripped (the expert confirmed the text gives no criterion for what transfers, so the transfer set is a stated choice, not a discovery), with an explicit honesty annotation on which principles are validated only by this soccer season. The episode-level principles are flagged as threshold-dependent because of the exchange-3 counterexample, so only match-scale structural principles are presented as generalizable.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Four domain-independent design principles, each stated as (mechanism, evidence status): P1 Connectivity floor — a team's coordination network should be kept near-complete at the working scale (n≈10-15 active members) so that any pair can coordinate directly; evidence: the Huskies' high density and stable clustering were present in wins and losses alike, i.e. necessary, not sufficient (status: necessary-condition, single-team). P2 Hub balance — concentrate coordination load on a small core (top ~4 members, Gini ≈ 0.3-0.45) but keep hub share below ~0.15 and maintain redundant second options for each core member's critical handoff; evidence: diversified M1/F2/M3/D1 spine plus the final-pass failure mode (status: mechanism inferred from the failure, not from a contrast). P3 Evaluate chains by endpoints — a sequence of contributions should be scored by where it terminates (outcome-adjacent position, leak mode), not by its internal fluency; formal form: indicator = f(terminal state), with internal structure only as a control variable (status: validated design rule; the episode-level instantiation is threshold-dependent per the counterexample, so the rule is stated at chain level). P4 Invariance is a finding, not a virtue — the same structure against every opponent (indicators stable across the 19 opponents) combined with an outcome gap means the structure is not adapting to counter-play; effective teams need a detectable, opponent-conditioned change in at least one indicator (status: negative result from this season). Required extensions for a genuinely generalized model: (i) an endogenous goal/outcome process (goals are the state that closes the funnel; the current data treats them as exogenous labels); (ii) pressure/opponent state — who is contesting, where, and at what intensity, which the pass data cannot see; (iii) time-varying capabilities (fatigue, substitutions — 114 substitution events are logged but not linked to capability); (iv) the non-identifiable possession-change process itself (the exchange-3 gap: a generalized model needs a stated ball-state process, not only events); (v) multi-team / population validation — one season of one team supports necessary-condition claims at best.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The transferable core: connectivity floor, hub balance with redundancy, endpoint-based scoring of contribution chains, and the invariance finding. What stays soccer-specific: the x-coordinate funnel, pass-type taxonomy, and the formation advice of Task 3. What the data cannot support, stated plainly: any claim that the Hubkies' structure caused wins (it is invariant across outcomes), any scale-free 'star team' generalization (Gini ≈ 0.3-0.47 is moderate, not heavy-tailed), and any tempo/flow claim finer than 10 minutes (the window evidence is confounded and the only significant window signal is threshold-dependent). The single most defensible general statement: at the ~10-15-member working scale, coordination networks that are dense, moderately hub-balanced, and whose chains are scored by endpoint are the substrate on which execution quality decides outcomes; structure sets the floor, endpoints decide the match. Limitations/bias: single team, single season, one sport; the principles are necessary-condition statements from a non-experimental setting, and the endpoint principle's soccer instantiation could not be validated because possession boundaries are not identifiable in the data.
